name: TCA peel
lead: A TCA peel is a chemical peel using trichloroacetic acid, generally classed as medium depth and performed in a clinic or surgical setting by a medical provider.[1] The acid coagulates skin proteins, causing controlled necrosis of the epidermis and upper dermis, followed by shedding and collagen remodelling.[2] As the old surface sheds and new skin forms, people see smoother texture, softer fine lines and, in some cases, more even tone, which is why peels are used for acne scars, sun-damaged skin and pigment.

Grokipedia describes TCA at roughly 10 to 50 percent as used for resurfacing in acne scars, fine wrinkles and photoaging, while stronger concentrations are used on individual lesions such as warts.[2] German dermatologist Paul Unna reported its use in peels in 1882.[2] The compound was first discovered by the French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas in 1839.[27] A focal variant called TCA CROSS applies high-strength acid inside individual atrophic scars, and a 2026 review of 34 publications reported improvement rates of 50 to 80 percent for ice pick and boxcar scars, with transient pigment change the most common adverse event.[28]

The published literature includes many small clinical studies and technique papers, covering photoaging, melasma, atrophic acne scars and pigmented lesions. In July 2024 the US FDA warned against using certain TCA peel products without professional supervision because of burn and scarring risks.[2]

paras: TCA is a caustic acid that precipitates proteins; in peels this causes controlled injury to the epidermis and upper dermis, followed by exfoliation and remodelling.[2][27] Wikipedia's chemical peel article classes TCA as a medium-depth peel and says medium-depth peels must be performed by a medical provider; patients usually feel warmth or burning, and unlike phenol, TCA has no numbing effect on the skin, so a tranquilizer and an oral analgesic may be used.[1]

Depth depends on the concentration, the number of coats, how the skin is prepared and how firmly it is applied; one 1994 paper noted that technique is more critical in medium-depth peeling than in deeper peels because of the variable penetration of TCA.[9] A review of TCA peels in Aesthetic Surgery Journal covers technique and indications.[21]

Wikipedia describes chemical peels as a depth ladder: light peels with alpha or beta hydroxy acids such as glycolic and salicylic acid are common in offices and med spas, medium peels such as TCA are done in offices or outpatient surgical centers, and deep peels, historically phenol-croton oil based, are the most intense; deeper peels carry more risk, and home kits may also cause injury or scarring.[1] Chemical resurfacing itself dates to the second half of the nineteenth century, when Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra introduced it using agents such as phenol and croton oil.[1]

Studies and registered trials have examined TCA peels for photoaged skin and actinic keratoses,[3] atrophic acne scars,[4] melasma,[5] benign pigmented lesions in darker skin,[6] and hand lentigines.[7] Researchers have also tested it for wrinkles at the corners of the eyes with or without botulinum toxin pretreatment.[26] Facial resurfacing for prevention of non-melanoma skin cancer has been examined in a randomised trial.[25]
Concentrated TCA is also used by clinicians on individual lesions such as warts.[2][27] The Resurfacing the acne-scarred face review discusses peels alongside other resurfacing methods for scars.[22]

A 2025 review of acne scarring describes a growing trend toward combination therapies that pair chemical peels, lasers and dermal fillers.[29] Sources describe TCA peels as aimed at the appearance of skin texture and tone rather than at facial structure.[1][21]

Because penetration of TCA varies, authors have described combination methods intended to make depth more predictable: Jessner's solution followed by TCA, developed by Monheit as a medium-depth peel for photoaged skin, actinic keratoses and superficial acne scars, in which degreasing and the combination allow deeper penetration of 35% TCA;[3][8] 70% glycolic acid followed by 35% TCA;[9] and a standardized TCA-based Blue Peel with depth control.[10] Pretreatment with tretinoin was reported in a randomized study to accelerate healing after TCA peeling.[11] Other trials compare TCA with fractional laser or microneedling.[12][18]

For darker skin, a 2004 paper described a focal TCA method for benign pigmented lesions,[6] and a 2017 paper described a technique intended for both light and dark skin.[14] Comparative work includes glycolic acid versus Jessner's-TCA peels in a clinical and histologic evaluation.[23]

Clinicians apply medium-strength TCA, often 15 to 35 percent in the published studies, across the face to treat photodamage, fine wrinkles and uneven pigment, sometimes after a Jessner's solution or glycolic acid step that increases penetration.[3][8][9] A double-blind study found a 35 percent peel healed faster after tretinoin pretreatment.[11]

Chemical Reconstruction of Skin Scars (CROSS) places concentrated TCA into narrow ice pick or boxcar acne scars rather than over the whole face, aiming to stimulate collagen within the scar. The 2026 review of 34 publications (937 patients) found it used mainly for ice pick and boxcar scars, reported improvement rates of 50 to 80 percent, and noted that multiple sessions gave greater improvement while higher concentrations raised complication risk; the authors concluded that it is a safe and effective option for atrophic scars.[28]

Studies pair TCA with microneedling, subcision, fractional laser, microdermabrasion or topical ascorbic acid.[4][5][12][18] A 2026 meta-analysis of 11 trials (713 participants) comparing microneedling with chemical peels for atrophic acne scars found no significant difference in clinically significant improvement, with peels causing burning and exfoliation and microneedling more procedural pain.[29]

Chemical peels as a group are associated with photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia and textural change, with complications rising with depth; medium peels cause warmth or burning and clinicians may use oral analgesics or topical anesthetics.[1] A comparison of two topical anesthetics for medium-depth peeling was published in 2000.[13] Concentrated TCA is classed as causing severe skin burns and eye damage, and China has prohibited it as a cosmetic ingredient.[2][27] Authors of a 2017 paper noted that fear of pigmentary complications and scarring leads many physicians to avoid TCA peels in darker skin, and described a technique intended for light and dark skin.[14]
In July 2024 the US FDA warned against using certain TCA peel products without professional supervision because of burn and scarring risks.[2]

Grokipedia lists redness, crusting and potential scarring as side effects, notes that China prohibits TCA as a cosmetic ingredient with consumer warnings dating from 2021, and says no outright ban on TCA in US consumer products was found.[2] In the 2026 CROSS review the most common adverse event was transient post-inflammatory pigment change.[28]

A 1989 report described the Jessner's + TCA peel as effective for photoaging, actinic keratoses and wrinkles.[3] A double-blind study in 16 older men (mean age 67) found tretinoin pretreatment accelerated healing after a 35% TCA peel.[11] A 2014 study of 50 patients with atrophic acne scars combined subcision, microneedling and 15% TCA peel.[4] Comparative studies have examined TCA with ascorbic acid for melasma.[5]

A meta-analysis of chemical peels as single agents for melasma in darker skin, covering ten randomised trials and three prospective comparative studies with 478 patients, found a difference favouring glycolic acid over TCA in the melasma area and severity index (mean difference -1.89).[17] A randomized trial of 40 women compared bimonthly 25% TCA with and without microneedling in melasma,[18] and a split-face study compared 15% TCA with 1550 nm fractional laser for melasma in Asian skin.[24]

For actinic keratoses, a randomised trial compared 35% TCA peel with ALA photodynamic therapy,[19] and a systematic review of field cancerisation treatment reports that, in one randomised comparison, ALA-PDT showed more clinical improvement than the TCA peel.[20]
Registered trials compare TCA with Jessner's solution for melasma,[15] with fractional laser,[12] and with intralesional saline for acne scars.[16] Many studies are small and use differing protocols.

TCA was discovered by Jean-Baptiste Dumas in 1839, and Paul Unna reported its use in peels in 1882.[27][2] The Jessner's-TCA combination was described by Monheit in 1989, the glycolic-TCA peel in 1994 and the Blue Peel in 1999.[3][9][10]

TCA peeling sits in the skin-focused part of looksmaxxing, where members discuss resurfacing acne scars and pigment. At least one looksmax.org thread asks members who have tried do-it-yourself TCA peels about their experience, which places the practice in the territory the FDA's 2024 warning addresses: certain TCA peel products used without professional supervision.[2] The comparison members draw is usually between clinic peels, home application and other scar treatments such as microneedling and lasers, which are the alternatives the published trials also compare.[12][18][29]
No published studies have examined home application by non-professionals, and the clinical literature describes physician-administered peels with pre-treatment, depth control and aftercare.[1][3][10]

card.summary: A medium-depth acid peel with decades of small clinical studies for scars, pigment and photoaging, and a real burn and scarring risk when done wrongly.
card.note: FDA warned in 2024 against certain TCA peel products used without professional supervision.

quick.overview:
A TCA peel applies trichloroacetic acid to the face to cause controlled injury, so damaged outer skin sheds and new skin forms. It is used for photoaging, acne scars and pigment.

Studies are mostly small, but the technique has been described in the literature since the 1980s.
quick.mechanism: TCA coagulates skin proteins in the epidermis and upper dermis, followed by shedding and collagen remodelling.
quick.risks: Redness, crusting, pigment change and scarring are documented; the FDA issued a warning in 2024 about unsupervised use of certain products.

chain: Concentrated acid causes a controlled injury to the outer skin
Skin sheds and rebuilds collagen over days to weeks
Smoother texture, softer acne scars and fine lines, more even pigmentation
angle.text: A clinician applies TCA to make the skin renew itself, which is used for photoaging, atrophic acne scars and pigmentation such as melasma. Depth rises with strength, so the strength and technique determine both the result and the downtime.
